Plants grow well enough in the dirt that god intended. The thing with soil is that if you take manage it wisely, it gets better every year - and the trees and perennials you plant in it become low-maintenance sources of food.

Nature wants to live - whether or not you exist, a seed wants to drop in the ground and grow into a plant that produces its next generation. And millions of years of evolution has resulted in a symbiotic system that is highly adapted and geared for production, with little interference from you. When you garden naturally, you are merely dipping your hand into the flowing stream of nature, and harvesting the gifts.

This is the main issue I have with hydroponics or other entirely artificial systems -- they require you to go to great effort to create and nurture the conditions in which the seed grows and reaches maturity. Having experimented with it, I find that it is simply not worth the trouble for me, because natural gardening is so much less dependent on my hands, my chemical feed, and my electronics as the life-support system for an otherwise healthy plant.

I grew cherry tomatoes, a few peppers, and a lot of greens quite successfully in a hydroponic setup.

The results were less impressive with strawberries, small carrots and peas.

It was a complete failure with full-size tomatoes (in a hydroponic 5-gallon container), figs, moringa, and a few other things I experimented with.

None of them turned a net-profit (in a small scale home setup) when I included input material costs. Without even including my time, or the cost of indoor space at market rents.
